title: The Good Shepherd and His Flock
overview: Jesus describes himself as the shepherd who truly cares for his people, and his claims about his closeness to God split his listeners and nearly get him stoned.

parts.label: Shepherd versus thief (vv. 1-6)
parts.note: Sheep were often kept in a walled pen with a gatekeeper, and a real shepherd came in openly, called each sheep by name and walked ahead of them. Jesus says this right after religious leaders had thrown out the blind man he healed in chapter 9, so most readers take it as a contrast between leaders who exploit people and one who truly cares.

parts.label: I am the gate (vv. 7-10)
parts.note: Jesus shifts the picture: he is the way into safety and good pasture, a life that is full rather than just survived. The 'thieves and robbers' who came before are usually taken as leaders who used people for their own ends, not the earlier prophets, though exactly whom he meant is not certain.

parts.label: The good shepherd (vv. 11-21)
parts.note: A hired worker runs when a wolf comes, but the true shepherd will die for the flock, and Jesus says he gives his life freely and will take it up again, which Christians read as pointing to his death and resurrection. The 'other sheep' are usually understood as non-Jewish people joining one flock, and the crowd splits: some call him mad, while others answer that a demon could not give sight to the blind.

parts.label: At the winter festival (vv. 22-30)
parts.note: The Festival of Dedication, now called Hanukkah, marked the cleansing of the Temple around 164 BC after a foreign king had defiled it, and here people press Jesus to say plainly whether he is the Messiah, the king God had promised. He points to his deeds, says no one can take his people from his hand or his Father's, and ends with 'I and the Father are one,' which Christians have long read as a claim to share God's own nature.

parts.label: Accused of blasphemy (vv. 31-39)
parts.note: Blasphemy means speaking against God or dishonoring him, and the specific charge here, which could bring death by stoning, is that a man was making himself God. Jesus quotes Psalm 82, where the word 'gods' is used of those who received God's word, usually understood as human leaders, and argues that if Scripture can say that, calling himself God's Son is no blasphemy, especially given his works.

parts.label: Retreat across the Jordan (vv. 40-42)
parts.note: Jesus escapes and goes back to the place where John the Baptist had first worked. People there notice that John did no miracles, yet what he said about Jesus proved true, and many believe.

think: Whose voice do you trust enough to follow, and what earned that trust?
